question_text: Based on the vignette, what is the MOST appropriate short-term physiotherapy goal to improve this boy's school participation over the next 6 weeks?
option_a: Achieve independent ambulation without assistive devices in the school hallway
option_b: Reduce hallway transit time by 25% using a consistent energy-conservation strategy with forearm crutches
option_c: Eliminate bilateral hip adductor spasticity through daily passive stretching
option_d: Transition the child to a manual wheelchair for all school mobility
rationale: A realistic, measurable short-term goal for a GMFCS III child is to improve functional efficiency in his current mobility context. Reducing transit time through an energy-conservation strategy is attainable, measurable, and school-relevant. Eliminating spasticity is not a realistic short-term PT goal; wheelchair transition contradicts the child's ambulatory capacity and participation goals.
vignette_text:
The following vignette is associated with the next 3 questions:

An 8-year-old boy with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy (GMFCS Level III) is seen for school-based physiotherapy. He ambulates with forearm crutches and ankle-foot orthoses bilaterally. He has difficulty navigating the school hallway between classes due to fatigue and requires 2× longer than peers. Spasticity: bilateral hip adductors and gastrocnemius Modified Ashworth Scale 2. He is able to participate in adapted physical education.

question_text: The boy's gastrocnemius spasticity is rated Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS) 2 bilaterally. What does this rating indicate?
option_a: No increase in muscle tone above normal
option_b: A slight increase in tone with a catch and release or minimal resistance at the end of range
option_c: More marked increase in tone, but the limb is still easily moved through most of the range of motion
option_d: Considerable increase in tone; passive movement is difficult
rationale: MAS 2 is defined as a more marked increase in muscle tone through most of the ROM, but the affected part can still be easily moved. MAS 1 is a slight increase with a catch and release; MAS 1+ has a catch and minimal resistance through less than half the ROM; MAS 3 is considerable increase with difficult passive movement.

question_text: What is the PRIMARY biomechanical benefit of bilateral solid ankle-foot orthoses (AFOs) for this child with spastic diplegia?
option_a: Prevent hip adductor contracture development
option_b: Control excessive ankle plantarflexion and promote a more energy-efficient gait pattern
option_c: Strengthen the tibialis anterior through resistive dorsiflexion
option_d: Reduce the need for forearm crutches over time
rationale: Solid AFOs control ankle plantarflexion during stance and swing, correcting equinus and crouch gait patterns. This reduces energy cost of ambulation and improves foot clearance — the primary mechanical rationale. AFOs do not directly address hip adductors or strengthen muscles; their relationship to upper-limb assistive device use is indirect.

question_text: Based on the vignette, what is the MOST appropriate initial physiotherapy intervention for this patient's acute pain management?
option_a: Begin lumbar flexion exercises to restore mobility and reduce pain
option_b: Educate on pain-free positioning, log-roll technique, and provide a thoracolumbar orthosis referral
option_c: Apply lumbar traction to decompress the fractured vertebra
option_d: Prescribe high-intensity core strengthening in the acute phase
rationale: Acute management of osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture (VCF) prioritizes pain control through positioning education (supine with pillow under knees), safe movement strategies (log-roll), and orthotic support. Flexion exercises and traction are contraindicated. High-intensity strengthening is inappropriate acutely and kinesiophobia must be addressed progressively.
vignette_text:
The following vignette is associated with the next 3 questions:

A 78-year-old woman presents to outpatient PT with a 2-week history of severe mid-back pain (7/10) following a minor fall at home. She has no neurological symptoms. X-ray confirms L1 compression fracture with 30% vertebral height loss. DEXA T-score: -3.1 (lumbar spine). She is taking calcium and vitamin D. She is fearful of movement and rates her pain as 7/10 with any position change.

question_text: Which spinal movements should be AVOIDED in this patient's physiotherapy program due to her osteoporotic compression fracture?
option_a: Thoracic extension and side-lying positioning
option_b: Spinal flexion, rotation, and combined loading movements
option_c: Isometric gluteal and transversus abdominis activation
option_d: Supine hip flexion within pain-free range
rationale: Spinal flexion increases anterior compressive forces on already-compromised vertebral bodies and dramatically increases fracture risk. Rotation and combined loading also increase fracture risk. Extension-based movement is generally safer for VCF. Isometric core and supine hip exercises within pain-free limits are appropriate.

question_text: For long-term osteoporosis management following recovery from her VCF, which exercise type has the MOST evidence for improving bone mineral density?
option_a: Aquatic therapy and swimming
option_b: Progressive resistance training and impact loading (e.g., stepping, jumping) appropriate to ability
option_c: Passive stretching and range-of-motion exercises
option_d: Low-intensity cycling on a stationary bike
rationale: Weight-bearing, progressive resistance, and impact exercises generate osteogenic mechanical signals that stimulate bone remodelling. Swimming and cycling are non-weight-bearing and have minimal effect on BMD. Passive stretching has no osteogenic effect. Impact must be graded to fracture risk but remains the most evidence-supported stimulus for BMD improvement.

question_text: Based on the vignette, what is the MOST likely diagnosis, and what does the vital capacity of 1.1 L (26% predicted) indicate about respiratory management?
option_a: Multiple sclerosis; the VC indicates moderate respiratory compromise requiring BiPAP weaning
option_b: Guillain-Barré syndrome; the VC below 20 mL/kg indicates high risk of respiratory failure requiring readiness for intubation
option_c: Myasthenia gravis; the VC indicates need for immediate tracheostomy
option_d: Critical illness polyneuropathy; the VC indicates safe tolerance for upright positioning and early mobilization
rationale: Ascending flaccid paralysis post-GI illness with facial weakness is classic Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS). The '20-30-40 rule' flags respiratory failure risk: VC <20 mL/kg (~1.4 L for average adult), MIP <30 cmH2O, MEP <40 cmH2O. This patient's VC of 1.1 L (26% predicted) indicates critical respiratory compromise with high intubation risk.
vignette_text:
The following vignette is associated with the next 3 questions:

A 45-year-old male was admitted to the ICU 10 days ago with ascending flaccid paralysis following a GI illness. He is currently on BiPAP (IPAP 14, EPAP 6) with FiO2 0.35. Vital capacity: 1.1L (predicted 4.2L). He has no independent respiratory effort and has bilateral facial weakness. He received IVIG 5 days ago. Limb strength: all extremities 1-2/5. He is afebrile and hemodynamically stable on no vasopressors.

question_text: What is the MOST appropriate physiotherapy intervention for this ICU patient at this stage of his illness?
option_a: Begin aggressive active-resisted exercises to all limbs to prevent deconditioning
option_b: Passive ROM, positioning to prevent contracture, and careful respiratory physiotherapy with BiPAP monitoring
option_c: Initiate tilt-table standing to promote early weight-bearing
option_d: Provide therapeutic ultrasound to the gastrocnemius to prevent DVT
rationale: In the acute GBS phase with severe weakness (1-2/5) and respiratory compromise on BiPAP, PT focuses on passive ROM to prevent contracture, careful positioning, skin protection, and respiratory care including assisted cough and secretion clearance. Active resisted exercise and orthostatic challenges are inappropriate with hemodynamic instability risk and severe weakness.

question_text: Which autonomic complication is MOST critical to monitor for in this patient with Guillain-Barré syndrome?
option_a: Hyperreflexia and clonus
option_b: Autonomic dysreflexia with blood pressure spikes above 180 mmHg systolic
option_c: Cardiac arrhythmias, blood pressure lability, and orthostatic hypotension
option_d: Hyperthermia and diaphoresis from spinal cord autonomic release
rationale: GBS frequently involves autonomic nervous system dysfunction: cardiac arrhythmias (including bradycardia and tachycardia), hypertensive and hypotensive swings, and orthostatic hypotension are the most life-threatening complications. Autonomic dysreflexia is a spinal cord injury phenomenon. Hyperreflexia is not seen in GBS (which causes hyporeflexia/areflexia).

question_text: Based on the vignette, what is the PRIMARY surgical rationale for restricting resisted external rotation until 12 weeks after supraspinatus repair?
option_a: The infraspinatus is the primary ER muscle and must be protected from co-contraction
option_b: Resisted ER places tensile load directly on the supraspinatus repair site via superior capsular tension
option_c: The patient's pain levels at 2/10 indicate that the tendon is not yet ready for any loading
option_d: Early resisted ER causes shoulder impingement under the coracoacromial arch
rationale: Resisted ER engages the posterior cuff muscles and creates superior shear and tensile forces at the supraspinatus footprint repair. During healing phase (weeks 6-12), the repair is at its weakest biologically (collagen remodelling) despite pain subsiding. Protecting the repair from tensile overload prevents re-tear. The infraspinatus distinction is secondary.
vignette_text:
The following vignette is associated with the next 3 questions:

A 52-year-old recreational tennis player presents to outpatient PT 8 weeks following surgical repair of a medium full-thickness supraspinatus tear (right dominant). The surgeon has cleared the patient to progress from passive to active-assisted range of motion. Current ROM (passive): flexion 120°, abduction 100°, ER 40°. Strength: not formally tested yet — surgeon note states 'no resisted external rotation until 12 weeks.' The patient is pain-free at rest with 2/10 with movement.

question_text: What is the MOST appropriate exercise progression at 8 weeks post-supraspinatus repair for this patient?
option_a: Full active resisted shoulder press and resisted ER with theraband
option_b: Active-assisted ROM exercises (pulleys, wand) within pain-free range and gentle scapular stabilization
option_c: Return to tennis serves to restore sport-specific function
option_d: Aggressive joint mobilization to the glenohumeral joint to restore end-range motion
rationale: At 8 weeks, surgeons typically progress from passive to AAROM (pulleys, wand exercises). Scapular stabilization (protraction/retraction/depression) can begin without loading the repair. Resisted rotator cuff exercises, sports-specific activity, and aggressive GH mobilization are all premature at this stage.

question_text: What is the expected ROM milestone that most rotator cuff repair protocols target by 12 weeks post-operatively?
option_a: Full passive ROM equal to the contralateral shoulder
option_b: Shoulder flexion to 90° and abduction to 60° with pain-free AROM
option_c: Full AROM: flexion 160-170°, abduction 150-160°, ER 60-70°
option_d: No ROM restrictions — full unrestricted motion expected by 12 weeks
rationale: By 12 weeks, most medium-tear repair protocols expect full or near-full AROM (flexion 160-170°, abduction 150-160°, ER 60-70°) and transition to active resisted exercises and strengthening. Full passive ROM is typically expected earlier (by 8-10 weeks); full AROM follows as active muscle control is re-established.

question_text: Based on the vignette, what is the PRIMARY goal of physiotherapy prehabilitation before this patient's TKA?
option_a: Eliminate bilateral knee pain before surgery
option_b: Optimize quadriceps strength and physical function to improve post-operative recovery speed and outcomes
option_c: Achieve normal BMI before surgery to reduce anesthetic risk
option_d: Delay surgery by improving symptoms sufficiently to avoid TKA
rationale: Prehabilitation before TKA targets preoperative strength (particularly quadriceps) and functional capacity. Evidence shows that higher preoperative quadriceps strength and better functional scores (e.g., chair stand, 6MWT) predict faster recovery and better 3/6-month outcomes. Prehab is not intended to eliminate pain or negate surgery.
vignette_text:
The following vignette is associated with the next 3 questions:

A 67-year-old retired postal worker with bilateral knee osteoarthritis is referred to PT for prehabilitation 8 weeks before right total knee arthroplasty. BMI: 38. Bilateral knee X-ray: Kellgren-Lawrence Grade 3 medial compartment OA. Quadriceps strength: right 3+/5, left 4/5. He reports pain 5/10 with walking >1 block, stiffness for 30 minutes in the morning. 30-second chair stand: 6 repetitions (age-norm: 14).

question_text: Which exercise is MOST appropriate to target the chair stand deficit and improve quadriceps strength in this patient during prehabilitation?
option_a: Full-arc knee extensions on a leg extension machine with heavy load
option_b: Sit-to-stand training with progressive reduction in seat height and addition of load
option_c: High-impact plyometric jump squats to maximize recruitment
option_d: Passive knee flexion stretching to improve range of motion
rationale: Sit-to-stand training directly targets the functional movement tested by the chair stand assessment and loads the quadriceps in a task-specific pattern. Progressions (lower seat, adding weight) allow dosage without excessive knee loading. Full-arc knee extensions place high patellofemoral stress; plyometrics are inappropriate with Grade 3 OA and pain; stretching does not build strength.

question_text: What does the current best evidence indicate about the effect of prehabilitation on post-TKA outcomes?
option_a: Prehabilitation consistently reduces the need for inpatient rehabilitation and eliminates post-operative strength deficits
option_b: Prehabilitation improves preoperative function and may modestly improve short-term post-operative recovery, but long-term outcomes are similar to no prehab
option_c: Prehabilitation has no measurable effect on post-TKA outcomes and is not recommended by clinical guidelines
option_d: Prehabilitation improves outcomes only when combined with nutritional supplementation
rationale: Systematic reviews (e.g., Chesham 2017, Matassi 2014) show prehabilitation improves preoperative strength/function and may improve early (3-month) recovery. Long-term (6-12 month) outcomes tend to converge between groups. Prehab is nonetheless recommended by many guidelines because of short-term benefits, reduced anxiety, and potential to reduce inpatient LOS.

question_text: A 35-year-old male runner presents with 6 weeks of anterior knee pain, worse with stair descent and prolonged sitting. Pain is reproduced by Clarke's test and patellar compression. Q-angle is 18°. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?
option_a: Patellar tendinopathy
option_b: Patellofemoral pain syndrome
option_c: Medial meniscus tear
option_d: Hoffa's fat pad impingement
rationale: Anterior knee pain worsened by stair descent, prolonged sitting (theatre sign), positive Clarke's test, and patellar compression in a runner with elevated Q-angle is classic patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS). Patellar tendinopathy presents at the inferior pole with load-related pain; meniscus tears have joint-line tenderness and positive McMurray's.

question_text: A 28-year-old female volleyball player presents with inferior pole patellar pain rated 6/10 during jumping and running, but 0/10 at rest. Victorian Institute of Sport Assessment-Patella (VISA-P) score is 52/100. The MOST evidence-based treatment is:
option_a: Complete rest from all loading activities for 6 weeks
option_b: Heavy slow resistance training (HSR) with progressive tendon loading
option_c: Corticosteroid injection followed by 2 weeks of rest
option_d: Patellar taping alone for symptom management
rationale: Heavy slow resistance (HSR) training is the gold standard for patellar tendinopathy, with strong evidence from RCTs (Kongsgaard et al.). It produces superior structural and symptomatic outcomes compared to eccentric-only programs. Complete rest is counterproductive. Corticosteroid injections are not recommended for tendinopathy and may be harmful long-term.

question_text: During the Ottawa Knee Rules assessment, which finding would INDICATE radiography for knee injury?
option_a: Knee pain with prolonged walking and crepitus
option_b: Isolated tenderness of the patella with no other bony tenderness
option_c: Inability to weight-bear for four steps immediately after injury and in the ED
option_d: Mild effusion with full active range of motion
rationale: Ottawa Knee Rules indicate X-ray if: age ≥55, isolated patella tenderness (no other bony), fibular head tenderness, inability to flex to 90°, OR inability to weight-bear four steps. Inability to weight-bear four steps immediately and in the ED is a clear Ottawa positive criterion.

question_text: A 42-year-old female presents with insidious onset lateral elbow pain for 3 months. Pain is reproduced with wrist extension against resistance and grip activities. Cozen's test is positive. Which structure is PRIMARILY involved?
option_a: Lateral ulnar collateral ligament
option_b: Extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) tendon
option_c: Radial nerve at the radial tunnel
option_d: Common flexor tendon origin
rationale: Lateral epicondylalgia (tennis elbow) involves degenerative tendinopathy of the ECRB at its origin on the lateral epicondyle. Positive Cozen's test (resisted wrist extension) confirms ECRB involvement. Radial tunnel syndrome involves the radial nerve and typically causes pain 4-5 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle. The common flexor tendon is medial.

question_text: A 55-year-old woman presents with gradual onset right shoulder pain over 6 months. Passive external rotation is 30° (contralateral 70°). All passive movements are restricted and painful at end-range. Rotator cuff strength is 5/5 when tested in available range. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?
option_a: Full-thickness rotator cuff tear
option_b: Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)
option_c: Subacromial impingement syndrome
option_d: Glenohumeral osteoarthritis
rationale: Adhesive capsulitis presents with insidious onset, global passive ROM restriction (especially ER > abduction > IR — the capsular pattern), and preserved rotator cuff strength within available range. Full-thickness tears typically show strength deficits. Impingement does not cause global passive restriction. OA would show X-ray changes.

question_text: A 19-year-old hockey player sustains an acute ACL tear and elects non-operative management. Which functional criterion is MOST important before return to sport?
option_a: Full passive range of motion restored to the injured knee
option_b: Limb symmetry index (LSI) ≥90% on quadriceps and hamstring strength testing and hop tests
option_c: Absence of joint effusion at rest
option_d: Completion of 6 months of physiotherapy regardless of functional status
rationale: Return-to-sport criteria for ACL injury require LSI ≥90% on strength (quad/hamstring isokinetics) and functional hop tests (single leg, triple hop, crossover hop). Time alone is insufficient; functional criteria reduce re-injury risk. Full passive ROM and absence of effusion are prerequisites but not sufficient RTS criteria.

question_text: A 68-year-old man had a left MCA ischemic stroke 3 weeks ago. He presents with right hemiplegia, global aphasia, and right hemianopia. Which communication strategy is MOST appropriate for physiotherapy sessions?
option_a: Speak loudly and slowly in the patient's right ear to compensate for hemianopia
option_b: Use simple yes/no questions, gesture, demonstration, and approach from the patient's left (unaffected) visual field
option_c: Limit sessions to 10 minutes due to global aphasia rendering communication impossible
option_d: Use written instructions only, as global aphasia spares written comprehension
rationale: Global aphasia affects all language modalities (speaking, comprehension, reading, writing). Effective strategies include short simple sentences, gesture, facial expression, demonstration, picture boards, and approaching from the intact visual field (left side, given right hemianopia). Written instructions are also impaired in global aphasia.

question_text: A 72-year-old woman with Parkinson's disease (Hoehn and Yahr Stage 3) has a falls history of 3 falls in the past 6 months. Which physiotherapy intervention has the STRONGEST evidence for falls reduction in this population?
option_a: Passive range-of-motion exercises performed by a caregiver daily
option_b: High-intensity progressive balance training and treadmill gait training
option_c: Nordic walking with poles to improve gait stability
option_d: Aquatic therapy for proprioceptive stimulation
rationale: High-intensity progressive balance and gait training (including treadmill training with or without LSVT BIG principles) has the strongest RCT evidence for reducing falls and improving gait in PD. Passive ROM, aquatic, and walking aids show benefit but not the same level of evidence for falls reduction specifically.

question_text: During a physiotherapy session, a patient with a T6 complete SCI (AIS A) develops a sudden headache (9/10), profuse diaphoresis above the level of injury, and blood pressure of 195/110 mmHg. What is the IMMEDIATE first action?
option_a: Apply ice pack to the forehead and call the physician for pain management
option_b: Sit the patient upright, check for and remove any noxious stimulus below the injury level, and call for emergency assistance
option_c: Lay the patient supine, elevate legs, and monitor blood pressure every 5 minutes
option_d: Administer sublingual nitroglycerin from the emergency cart
rationale: This is autonomic dysreflexia (AD) — a hypertensive emergency in SCI above T6. Immediate management: sit upright (lowering BP through orthostatic effect), identify and remove noxious stimuli below injury level (full bladder, bowel, skin pressure), loosen clothing, and call emergency assistance. Supine positioning dangerously raises BP. Nitroglycerin administration requires physician order.

question_text: A physiotherapist is completing a Berg Balance Scale assessment on a 75-year-old man post-stroke. He scores 38/56. What fall risk category does this score indicate?
option_a: Low fall risk — no intervention required
option_b: Moderate fall risk — requires supervision and targeted balance training
option_c: High fall risk — requires assistive device and environmental modification
option_d: Unable to classify — the BBS is not validated for stroke populations
rationale: BBS scores: 0-20 = high fall risk; 21-40 = moderate fall risk; 41-56 = low fall risk. A score of 38 falls in the moderate fall risk range (21-40), indicating the need for supervised mobility, targeted balance training, and fall prevention strategies. The BBS is well-validated in stroke populations.

question_text: A 58-year-old male 6 weeks post-CABG is enrolled in Phase II cardiac rehabilitation. His resting HR is 62 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg. Which intensity guide is MOST appropriate for aerobic exercise prescription?
option_a: Target HR of 85% of age-predicted maximum (220 - age)
option_b: Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) 11-13/20 (Borg scale) or 40-60% heart rate reserve (Karvonen method)
option_c: Exercise until angina (4/10) is achieved, then rest
option_d: Walk at maximum comfortable pace for 30 consecutive minutes from Day 1
rationale: Phase II cardiac rehab targets moderate intensity: RPE 11-13 (Borg 6-20) or 40-60% HRR (Karvonen). Age-predicted max HR is unreliable post-CABG, especially on beta-blockers. Exercise to angina is never a target. Immediate high-volume exercise without progression is inappropriate in the early post-surgical phase.

question_text: A 65-year-old COPD patient (GOLD Stage 3) is assessed with the 6-Minute Walk Test. Which finding would be the MOST clinically meaningful change following an 8-week pulmonary rehabilitation program?
option_a: Improvement of 15 meters in 6MWT distance
option_b: Improvement of 35 meters or more in 6MWT distance (meeting the MCID)
option_c: Reduction in FEV1/FVC ratio from 0.52 to 0.48
option_d: Decrease in resting SpO2 from 94% to 91%
rationale: The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for 6MWT in COPD is approximately 25-35 meters. An improvement of 35m meets the MCID and represents a clinically meaningful change in functional exercise capacity. FEV1/FVC worsening is not a PT outcome. SpO2 decrease would be a negative finding.

question_text: A physiotherapist assesses a patient post-pneumonia with decreased breath sounds at the right base, dullness to percussion, and the patient is febrile. Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. Which airway clearance technique is MOST appropriate?
option_a: Postural drainage in the Trendelenburg (head-down) position
option_b: Active cycle of breathing technique (ACBT) in sitting or modified postural drainage positions
option_c: Mechanical ventilation with PEEP
option_d: High-frequency chest wall oscillation vest therapy
rationale: ACBT (breathing control → thoracic expansion exercises → forced expiration technique) is the most appropriate for community-acquired or post-pneumonia consolidation in a patient who can cooperate. Head-down Trendelenburg is often contraindicated in acute pneumonia due to risk of aspiration and hemodynamic effects. HFCWO is typically used in conditions like cystic fibrosis.

question_text: An absolute contraindication to exercise testing in a cardiac patient is:
option_a: Resting BP of 150/90 mmHg with no symptoms
option_b: Uncontrolled symptomatic heart failure with acute decompensation
option_c: History of myocardial infarction more than 6 weeks ago
option_d: Mild aortic stenosis with preserved exercise capacity
rationale: Acute decompensated heart failure is an absolute contraindication to exercise testing (AHA guidelines). Resting BP up to 200/110 mmHg is the threshold for absolute contraindication; 150/90 is not. Remote MI >6 weeks is not a contraindication. Mild aortic stenosis with preserved exercise capacity is a relative contraindication only when severe.

question_text: A patient with congestive heart failure (EF 30%) is participating in an outpatient exercise program. Which symptom should prompt IMMEDIATE exercise termination and emergency response?
option_a: RPE of 13/20 and mild dyspnea on exertion
option_b: New onset chest pain radiating to the jaw with diaphoresis and pallor
option_c: Heart rate increase from 68 to 95 bpm during warm-up
option_d: SpO2 drop from 97% to 94% during aerobic exercise
rationale: New onset chest pain with jaw radiation, diaphoresis, and pallor are cardinal signs of acute myocardial ischemia/infarction — a medical emergency requiring immediate exercise termination, patient positioning, calling emergency services, and activation of the emergency action plan. Mild dyspnea, expected HR rise, and minor SpO2 drop are expected and not emergency indicators.

question_text: A physiotherapist is treating a 16-year-old patient for knee rehabilitation. During treatment the patient discloses that they are being physically abused at home. What is the physiotherapist's MOST appropriate immediate action?
option_a: Maintain confidentiality and document the disclosure in the chart for future reference only
option_b: Report the suspected abuse to the appropriate child protective services authority as required by mandatory reporting obligations
option_c: Consult with the patient's parents before taking any action to ensure family involvement
option_d: Refer the patient to a social worker and take no further action
rationale: All Canadian provinces have mandatory reporting legislation requiring regulated health professionals to report suspected child abuse to child protective services. This obligation supersedes patient confidentiality and cannot be delegated. Consulting parents who may be the abusers is inappropriate. Referral alone does not discharge the mandatory reporting duty.

question_text: A physiotherapist disagrees with a physician's prescription for strict bed rest following a lumbar strain. The MOST professional action is:
option_a: Follow the physician's orders without question to maintain the therapeutic team hierarchy
option_b: Communicate concerns directly with the physician, citing current evidence that early mobilization reduces recovery time, and document the exchange
option_c: Disregard the bed rest order and begin mobilization based on physiotherapy clinical judgment alone
option_d: Discharge the patient from physiotherapy as there is no scope for intervention
rationale: Physiotherapists are autonomous professionals with a duty to advocate for evidence-based care. The appropriate response is professional interprofessional communication — expressing clinical concern to the physician with evidence, then documenting the discussion. Unilaterally disregarding physician orders without communication is unprofessional. Dismissal without advocacy fails the patient.

question_text: Which element of informed consent is MOST commonly overlooked in physiotherapy practice?
option_a: Disclosure of the physiotherapist's credentials
option_b: Disclosure of treatment alternatives (including no treatment) and associated risks and benefits
option_c: Verbal confirmation that the patient has signed the intake form
option_d: Confirmation that the patient is above 18 years of age
rationale: Informed consent requires: information disclosure (diagnosis, proposed treatment, risks, benefits, alternatives including no treatment), comprehension, voluntariness, and capacity. Disclosure of alternatives is a frequently underemphasized component. Signing an intake form does not constitute informed consent for specific interventions. Age of majority matters for capacity but is not the most commonly overlooked element.

question_text: A physiotherapist is approached by a colleague who appears visibly intoxicated before a patient treatment session. The MOST appropriate first action is:
option_a: Report directly to the provincial regulatory college without speaking to the colleague first
option_b: Speak to the colleague directly about the concern, ensure no patients are seen until the colleague is safe, and follow the organization's reporting protocol
option_c: Cover the colleague's patients for that session and not report to protect the colleague's career
option_d: Document the observation in the patient's chart and take no further action
rationale: Patient safety is paramount. The immediate priority is ensuring the colleague does not treat patients in an impaired state. The professional approach is direct communication with the colleague and following institutional protocols (supervisor, department head). Regulatory reporting may follow institutional processes. Covering without reporting enables unsafe practice.

question_text: A physiotherapy clinic owner instructs a physiotherapist to treat 6 patients simultaneously in an open gym setting. The physiotherapist's PRIMARY ethical obligation in this situation is:
option_a: Follow the clinic owner's instruction as they are the employer and have final authority
option_b: Ensure patient safety and quality of care are maintained; refuse or negotiate workloads that compromise professional standards
option_c: Treat 6 patients simultaneously and document each treatment session thoroughly to manage the risk
option_d: Resign immediately and report the clinic to the regulatory college
rationale: Physiotherapists are individually accountable for the quality and safety of care they provide. If simultaneous caseload compromises patient safety, the professional obligation is to raise concerns, negotiate, and if necessary refuse assignments that violate practice standards — regardless of employer authority. Employment relationships do not override professional and ethical obligations.

question_text: Under the ICF (International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health) framework, 'difficulty walking on uneven surfaces' is classified under which component?
option_a: Body Structure
option_b: Body Function
option_c: Activity
option_d: Participation
rationale: The ICF classifies functioning into Body Functions (physiological/psychological), Body Structures (anatomical), Activities (execution of tasks), and Participation (involvement in life situations). 'Walking on uneven surfaces' is a specific task execution — an Activity limitation. Participation would involve roles (e.g., inability to attend community events).

question_text: A 30-year-old male construction worker presents with acute low back pain (onset 3 days ago) with radiation to the left buttock. Straight leg raise is positive at 45° on the left, reproducing radicular pain to the dorsum of the foot. Neurological exam: decreased left Achilles reflex, weakness of ankle plantarflexion, decreased sensation along the lateral foot. Which nerve root is MOST likely affected?
option_a: L3
option_b: L4
option_c: L5
option_d: S1
rationale: S1 nerve root: decreased Achilles reflex (S1 myotome), weakness of gastrocnemius/plantarflexion, sensory deficit along lateral foot and plantar surface. L5 affects ankle dorsiflexion and great toe extension, with sensory loss over dorsum of foot and lateral leg. L4 affects knee extension and patellar reflex.

question_text: Which clinical finding would constitute a RED FLAG requiring immediate medical referral in a patient presenting with low back pain?
option_a: Morning stiffness lasting 45 minutes that improves with activity
option_b: New onset bilateral leg weakness and saddle anesthesia in a 45-year-old male
option_c: Pain worsening with prolonged sitting and relieved by walking
option_d: Positive FABER test with groin pain reproduction
rationale: Bilateral leg weakness and saddle anesthesia are cardinal signs of cauda equina syndrome (CES), a surgical emergency. CES also typically presents with bowel/bladder dysfunction. Immediate referral for MRI and surgical consultation is required. Morning stiffness improving with activity suggests inflammatory arthritis (red flag for different reason). FABER positive with groin pain suggests hip pathology.

question_text: A 22-year-old female soccer player sustains an acute grade II lateral ankle sprain (ATFL). At day 3, swelling is 2+ and she is weight-bearing with a limp. Which intervention is MOST appropriate at this stage?
option_a: Aggressive passive joint mobilization to restore full dorsiflexion
option_b: POLICE protocol (Protection, Optimal Loading, Ice, Compression, Elevation) with partial weight-bearing as tolerated
option_c: Immobilization in a plaster cast for 3 weeks
option_d: Isokinetic strength testing to determine baseline deficits
rationale: Current evidence supports POLICE (replacing RICE) in acute ankle sprain: protect from harmful loading, optimize loading through progressive weight-bearing, and use ice/compression/elevation for swelling. Grade II sprains do not require immobilization. Aggressive mobilization at day 3 is premature. Isokinetic testing is inappropriate in the acute inflammatory phase.

question_text: A physiotherapist performs a Lachman test on a 26-year-old male after a ski injury. There is a soft end-feel with 8 mm of anterior tibial translation. What does this finding indicate?
option_a: Grade I posterior cruciate ligament sprain
option_b: Grade III anterior cruciate ligament tear (complete)
option_c: Grade II medial collateral ligament sprain
option_d: Normal finding — 8 mm is within normal limits bilaterally
rationale: Lachman test assesses ACL integrity. Soft end-feel with >5 mm anterior tibial translation compared to the contralateral side indicates ACL injury. A soft end-feel with 8 mm translation suggests complete (Grade III) ACL tear. Grade I/II ACL sprains have firmer end-feels with less translation. Normal Lachman has firm end-feel with <3 mm translation.

question_text: A 47-year-old male office worker with chronic neck pain and right-sided C6 radiculopathy has decreased biceps reflex on the right, weakness in wrist extension (4/5), and paresthesia along the thumb and index finger. Which dermatome/myotome pattern confirms C6 involvement?
option_a: Decreased triceps reflex, finger extension weakness, ring and small finger paresthesia
option_b: Decreased biceps/brachioradialis reflex, wrist extension weakness, thumb-index finger paresthesia
option_c: Normal reflexes, shoulder abduction weakness, lateral arm paresthesia
option_d: Decreased patellar reflex, quadriceps weakness, medial knee paresthesia
rationale: C6 myotome: wrist extensors (ECRL/B), biceps. C6 reflex: biceps and brachioradialis. C6 dermatome: lateral forearm, thumb, index finger. This pattern perfectly matches the clinical presentation. C7 causes triceps reflex loss, elbow extension weakness, middle finger paresthesia. C5 causes deltoid/biceps weakness, lateral arm sensation, biceps reflex.

question_text: Which hip special test has the HIGHEST sensitivity for detecting labral tears and is therefore most useful as a screening test?
option_a: FABER (Patrick's test)
option_b: FADDIR (Flexion-Adduction-Internal Rotation) test
option_c: Trendelenburg test
option_d: Thomas test
rationale: FADDIR has high sensitivity (~75-95%) for intra-articular hip pathology including labral tears and femoroacetabular impingement. It is used as a screening test because its high sensitivity means a negative result helps rule out the condition. FABER has moderate sensitivity and specificity. Trendelenburg and Thomas tests assess muscle function, not labral integrity.

question_text: A 60-year-old male carpenter with a 2-year history of lateral hip pain describes pain with lying on the affected side, walking stairs, and crossing legs. Palpation reveals tenderness directly over the greater trochanter. MOST likely diagnosis?
option_a: Trochanteric bursitis (isolated)
option_b: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS) — likely gluteal tendinopathy
option_c: Iliotibial band syndrome
option_d: L4-L5 referred pain
rationale: Modern understanding recognizes 'trochanteric bursitis' as predominantly gluteal tendinopathy (gluteus medius/minimus) — termed Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome. Lying on the affected side, stair climbing, and compressive positions (crossing legs) all provoke tendon compression at the trochanter. Isolated bursitis is uncommon. ITB syndrome is typically more distal at the lateral femoral condyle.

question_text: A physiotherapist is assessing a 55-year-old female 6 months post right hemisphere stroke. She consistently bumps into objects on her left side, ignores food on the left half of the plate, and does not dress the left side of her body. Which condition does this describe?
option_a: Left homonymous hemianopia
option_b: Left unilateral spatial neglect (USN)
option_c: Left hemiplegia with sensory loss
option_d: Constructional apraxia
rationale: Unilateral spatial neglect (USN) following right hemisphere stroke causes failure to attend to, respond to, or orient toward stimuli on the contralesional (left) side. It is distinct from hemianopia (visual field loss). USN affects attention across multiple domains — visual, motor, representational — accounting for dressing and eating deficits. Hemiplegia involves motor loss; apraxia involves motor planning.

question_text: A 40-year-old female with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) presents with fatigue rated 8/10 on the Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS), heat sensitivity, and mild spasticity. She lives alone and works full-time. Which fatigue management strategy has the STRONGEST evidence?
option_a: Complete rest during all episodes of fatigue to conserve energy
option_b: Aerobic exercise at moderate intensity, energy conservation education, and cooling strategies
option_c: Daily passive stretching to reduce spasticity-related fatigue
option_d: High-intensity interval training to maximize cardiovascular fitness
rationale: Evidence-based MS fatigue management combines aerobic exercise (moderate intensity: 60-75% HRmax), energy conservation/activity pacing education, and cooling strategies (Uhthoff phenomenon management). Complete rest worsens deconditioning. High-intensity training is poorly tolerated in heat-sensitive MS. Stretching addresses spasticity but not primary MS fatigue.

question_text: A 30-year-old male with a T10 ASIA A SCI wishes to transfer independently from wheelchair to bed. Which muscle group is MOST critical for performing this lateral sliding transfer?
option_a: Hip flexors (iliopsoas)
option_b: Shoulder depressors and elbow extensors (serratus anterior, triceps)
option_c: Wrist flexors and finger flexors
option_d: Scapular retractors (rhomboids)
rationale: Independent lateral sliding transfers require the ability to depress the shoulder girdle (serratus anterior, lower trapezius) and extend the elbows (triceps) to lift the buttocks off the surface. At T10, triceps and serratus are intact. Hip flexors are paralyzed in T10 complete SCI. Wrist/finger flexion and scapular retraction are secondary.

question_text: Using the ASIA Impairment Scale (AIS), a patient with a spinal cord injury has intact motor and sensory function below the neurological level, and more than half of key muscles below the NLI have a muscle grade ≥3. What is their AIS classification?
option_a: AIS B — Sensory Incomplete
option_b: AIS C — Motor Incomplete
option_c: AIS D — Motor Incomplete
option_d: AIS E — Normal
rationale: AIS D: Motor incomplete — motor function is preserved below the NLI, and at least half of key muscle functions below the NLI have a muscle grade ≥3. AIS C differs in that less than half of key muscles have grade ≥3. AIS B is sensory-only preservation. AIS E indicates full neurological recovery.

question_text: A physiotherapist auscultates crackles (rales) at the right lower lung base in a post-operative patient on day 2 following abdominal surgery. SpO2 is 93% on room air. The MOST appropriate intervention is:
option_a: Notify the surgeon and await chest X-ray before initiating any intervention
option_b: Incentive spirometry, deep breathing exercises, ACBT, and early mobilization
option_c: Supine positioning with head of bed flat to maximize lung expansion
option_d: Aggressive percussion and postural drainage in Trendelenburg position
rationale: Post-operative atelectasis is common following abdominal surgery due to reduced diaphragmatic excursion and analgesia-induced splinting. First-line PT interventions include incentive spirometry, deep breathing exercises, ACBT, and early upright positioning/mobilization. Flat supine positioning reduces FRC. Trendelenburg postural drainage is not indicated for atelectasis and is poorly tolerated post-abdominally.

question_text: A mechanically ventilated patient in the ICU (mode: AC/VC, RR 14, TV 500 mL, PEEP 8, FiO2 0.5) is being considered for early mobilization. Which parameter would be an ABSOLUTE contraindication to initiating sitting at edge of bed?
option_a: FiO2 of 0.5
option_b: Mean arterial pressure of 55 mmHg on vasopressor support
option_c: Presence of an arterial line
option_d: PEEP of 8 cmH2O
rationale: ICU early mobilization is contraindicated with hemodynamic instability, including vasopressor-dependent hypotension (MAP <65 mmHg on vasopressors). FiO2 ≤0.6 and PEEP ≤10-12 cmH2O are generally considered safe for mobilization. Arterial lines are compatible with mobilization. MAP of 55 on vasopressors indicates circulatory instability precluding safe orthostatic challenge.

question_text: During a graded exercise test, a patient with stable coronary artery disease develops 2 mm horizontal ST-segment depression in leads V4-V6 at a workload of 6 METs. The physiotherapist should:
option_a: Continue the test as this is a normal exercise response
option_b: Terminate the test immediately and position the patient supine with legs elevated
option_c: Terminate the exercise test, cool down gradually, monitor ECG, and notify the supervising physician
option_d: Reduce workload to 3 METs and continue monitoring for further changes
rationale: ≥2 mm horizontal ST depression is an indication to terminate a graded exercise test. The patient should cool down gradually (abrupt cessation risks BP drop), ECG monitoring continued, and the supervising physician notified. Abrupt cessation and supine positioning can cause venous pooling. Reducing workload alone does not address significant ischemia.

question_text: A 50-year-old with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis presents to physiotherapy with acute wrist pain, swelling, and warmth. Which joint involvement pattern MOST distinguishes RA from osteoarthritis?
option_a: Involvement of the distal interphalangeal joints (DIPs)
option_b: Symmetric involvement of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints with morning stiffness >1 hour
option_c: Unilateral joint involvement with osteophyte formation
option_d: Episodic attacks with complete resolution between flares
rationale: RA characteristically involves MCPs and PIPs symmetrically with prolonged morning stiffness (>1 hour). DIP involvement is characteristic of OA and psoriatic arthritis. Unilateral OA with osteophytes is typical OA. Episodic attacks with complete resolution is gout. Morning stiffness in OA is typically <30 minutes.

question_text: A 38-year-old male presents with 3 months of insidious posterior heel pain, worse with the first steps in the morning and after prolonged sitting. Pain is located at the medial calcaneal tubercle and is reproduced with windlass test. MOST likely diagnosis?
option_a: Achilles tendinopathy
option_b: Plantar fasciitis (plantar fasciopathy)
option_c: Calcaneal stress fracture
option_d: Tarsal tunnel syndrome
rationale: Plantar fasciitis presents with medial calcaneal tubercle pain, post-static dyskinesia (morning pain and after sitting), positive windlass test (dorsiflexing toes reproduces pain). Achilles tendinopathy is posterior, not inferior. Calcaneal stress fracture shows positive squeeze test. Tarsal tunnel presents with burning/paresthesia along plantar foot.

question_text: A 25-year-old female competitive swimmer presents with right shoulder pain during the pull phase of freestyle. Hawkins-Kennedy and empty can tests are positive. Neer's sign is positive. Which diagnosis is MOST likely?
option_a: Acromioclavicular joint sprain
option_b: Subacromial impingement syndrome / supraspinatus tendinopathy
option_c: Long head of biceps tendinopathy
option_d: Glenohumeral instability
rationale: Positive Hawkins-Kennedy, Neer's sign, and empty can test together are classic for subacromial impingement with supraspinatus involvement. Swimming freestyle overhead imposes repetitive subacromial compression. AC joint sprain presents with AC joint tenderness. Biceps tendinopathy is more anteriorly located. Instability has positive apprehension/relocation tests.

question_text: The McKenzie classification identifies three pain syndromes. A patient whose pain is present only during specific postures (e.g., end-range lumbar flexion) and resolves immediately upon correction of posture — WITHOUT directional preference — is classified as which syndrome?
option_a: Derangement syndrome
option_b: Dysfunction syndrome
option_c: Postural syndrome
option_d: Spondylogenic syndrome
rationale: McKenzie Postural Syndrome: pain is produced by mechanical deformation of normal tissue due to end-range or sustained posture. Pain resolves immediately when posture is corrected. No movement loss, no directional preference. Dysfunction involves pain due to shortened adaptive tissue at end-range, not corrected by posture change alone. Derangement involves directional preference.

question_text: Which of the following BEST describes the physiotherapist's role during the 'outcome measurement' phase of the clinical reasoning process?
option_a: Select outcome measures based on the referring physician's preferences to maintain interprofessional relationships
option_b: Use valid, reliable, and responsive outcome measures linked to the patient's ICF domains to evaluate treatment effectiveness
option_c: Administer outcome measures only at discharge to determine overall goal achievement
option_d: Use global rating of change as the only required outcome measure
rationale: Outcome measures should be selected based on validity, reliability, responsiveness to change, and relevance to the patient's ICF domains (body function, activity, participation). They should be administered at baseline and follow-up to evaluate treatment effectiveness. Single-timepoint measurement and physician preference are not sound rationale.

question_text: What does 'therapeutic privilege' refer to in the context of informed consent, and is it ethically justified in physiotherapy practice?
option_a: A therapist's right to refuse treatment to a patient based on personal values
option_b: Withholding information from patients when the therapist believes knowledge would cause harm; it is generally NOT ethically justified in modern practice
option_c: A special consent exception for emergency procedures when a patient is unconscious
option_d: The right to use proprietary techniques without disclosing the theoretical basis to the patient
rationale: Therapeutic privilege refers to withholding information based on a paternalistic belief that disclosure would harm the patient. Modern bioethical standards and patient-centred care principles reject this approach — autonomy and full disclosure are paramount. Emergency exceptions (implied consent) are a separate concept. Conscientious objection concerns refusing treatment.

question_text: A physiotherapist is asked by the patient's insurer to provide a full copy of the clinical chart. The MOST appropriate action is:
option_a: Provide the full chart immediately as insurers have a legal right to all health information
option_b: Obtain written patient consent specifying what information may be released before disclosing any records to the insurer
option_c: Provide a verbal summary of treatment progress only to protect patient privacy
option_d: Decline entirely as all patient information is protected by physiotherapy-client privilege
rationale: Under PIPEDA and provincial privacy legislation, health information may only be disclosed to third parties (including insurers) with informed written patient consent specifying the scope of disclosure. Insurers do not have automatic right of access. Verbal summary alone is insufficient and not documented. Absolute non-disclosure regardless of consent is also incorrect.

question_text: A Maitland Grade IV joint mobilization is BEST described as:
option_a: Small amplitude oscillations at the beginning of the available range
option_b: Large amplitude oscillations through the full available range
option_c: Small amplitude oscillations at the end of the available range
option_d: A high-velocity thrust at the end of the available range
rationale: Maitland grades: I = small amplitude at beginning of range; II = large amplitude in middle of range; III = large amplitude reaching end of range; IV = small amplitude at end of range; V = manipulation (HVLA thrust). Grade IV is used to stretch stiff joints and break minor adhesions at end range.

question_text: In the Cyriax approach to musculoskeletal examination, a 'capsular pattern' of the shoulder refers to which restriction sequence?
option_a: Flexion > Abduction > External Rotation
option_b: External Rotation > Abduction > Internal Rotation
option_c: Abduction > Internal Rotation > External Rotation
option_d: Internal Rotation > External Rotation > Abduction
rationale: Cyriax's capsular pattern of the glenohumeral joint follows the sequence: External Rotation most restricted > Abduction > Internal Rotation least restricted. This pattern reflects the anatomical configuration of the GH capsule and its response to diffuse capsular inflammation or fibrosis. Deviation from this pattern suggests non-capsular or extra-articular pathology.

question_text: A 70-year-old man with idiopathic Parkinson's disease demonstrates festinating gait, reduced arm swing, and freeze of gait (FOG) when entering doorways. Which cueing strategy has the STRONGEST evidence for addressing freezing of gait?
option_a: Verbal counting to set cadence
option_b: Rhythmic auditory stimulation (RAS) and visual floor cues (transverse lines)
option_c: Asking the patient to walk faster to overcome the freeze
option_d: Using a rollator walker to improve gait security
rationale: Rhythmic auditory stimulation (metronome, music) and visual cues (floor transverse lines, laser from walking aids) have the strongest evidence for reducing FOG frequency and improving gait speed in PD. These bypass defective internal basal ganglia timing by providing external rhythmic drivers. Rollators may paradoxically worsen FOG. Verbal counting has some effect but less evidence than RAS.

question_text: A 55-year-old male is 6 months post right total hip arthroplasty (posterior approach) and presents to physiotherapy with a Trendelenburg gait. Which muscle is MOST likely responsible?
option_a: Iliopsoas — hip flexor weakness
option_b: Gluteus medius — hip abductor weakness on the stance limb
option_c: Quadriceps — knee extension weakness causing compensatory gait
option_d: Tensor fasciae latae — ITB tightness causing lateral trunk shift
rationale: Trendelenburg gait is characterized by contralateral pelvic drop during single-leg stance, caused by ipsilateral gluteus medius (hip abductor) weakness. Post-THA, the gluteus medius is commonly weakened due to surgical approach, disuse atrophy, or trochanteric involvement. The physiotherapy goal is to strengthen the ipsilateral hip abductors.

question_text: Which assessment tool is MOST appropriate to objectively measure functional exercise capacity in a patient with moderate COPD in an outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation setting?
option_a: Maximum oxygen uptake (VO2max) via cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET)
option_b: 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT)
option_c: 1-Repetition Maximum (1RM) testing for quadriceps
option_d: Spirometry (FEV1, FVC)
rationale: The 6MWT is the gold-standard field test for functional exercise capacity in COPD and pulmonary rehabilitation, with established MCID (25-35m), reliability, validity, and responsiveness. CPET requires specialized equipment and is used for diagnostic workup. 1RM tests muscle strength, not exercise capacity. Spirometry measures lung function, not functional capacity.

question_text: A 70-year-old male with a 5-year history of heart failure (NYHA Class II) is enrolled in cardiac rehabilitation. Which physiological adaptation MOST explains improved exercise tolerance following aerobic training?
option_a: Increased resting ejection fraction
option_b: Peripheral adaptations: increased oxidative enzyme capacity, skeletal muscle mitochondrial density, and improved endothelial function
option_c: Reduced heart rate at maximum exercise
option_d: Decreased ventricular wall thickness
rationale: In heart failure with reduced EF, aerobic training improves exercise tolerance primarily through peripheral adaptations: enhanced skeletal muscle oxidative capacity, mitochondrial biogenesis, and improved endothelial function reducing peripheral resistance. Ejection fraction does not consistently increase with training in HFrEF. Central cardiac adaptations (stroke volume) are more modest.

question_text: A 16-year-old female basketball player has right knee anterior pain worsened with activity. X-ray shows fragmentation of the tibial tubercle. She has point tenderness over the tibial tubercle and pain with resisted knee extension. MOST likely diagnosis?
option_a: Sinding-Larsen-Johansson syndrome
option_b: Osgood-Schlatter disease
option_c: Patellar tendinopathy
option_d: Bipartite patella
rationale: Osgood-Schlatter disease is an apophysitis of the tibial tubercle in adolescents, caused by repetitive traction of the patellar tendon during growth. It presents with tibial tubercle tenderness, X-ray fragmentation of the tibial tubercle, and pain with resisted extension. Sinding-Larsen-Johansson affects the inferior patellar pole. Patellar tendinopathy is in adults with load-related tendon pain.

question_text: A physiotherapist is assessing thoracic outlet syndrome in a 32-year-old female. Which combination of positive test findings MOST strongly suggests a neurogenic mechanism?
option_a: Positive Adson's test and radial pulse obliteration with arm elevation
option_b: Positive ULNT1, positive Roos test reproducing neurological symptoms, and weakness of intrinsic hand muscles
option_c: Positive Spurling's test at C6-7 with right shoulder pain radiation
option_d: Positive thoracic extension with rib hypomobility at T3-4
rationale: Neurogenic TOS (most common type) involves brachial plexus compression: ULNT1 reproducing arm symptoms, Roos test (90° abduction, ER, repeated hand gripping) causing neurological symptoms, and intrinsic hand weakness (C8-T1 distribution from lower trunk). Adson's with pulse obliteration suggests arterial TOS. Spurling's is cervical radiculopathy.

question_text: A 62-year-old male with chronic cerebellar ataxia (spinocerebellar ataxia) presents for balance rehabilitation. He has wide-based gait, intention tremor, dysmetria, and dysdiadochokinesia. Which balance training component is MOST important for this patient?
option_a: Vestibular habituation exercises performed in head-down positions
option_b: Task-specific coordination training with progressive reduction in base of support and dual-task challenges
option_c: Strengthening of dorsiflexors and invertors to improve proprioceptive input
option_d: Cognitive-motor dual-task training using arithmetic while standing on foam
rationale: Cerebellar ataxia rehabilitation uses task-specific coordination training that targets the timing and sequencing deficits characteristic of cerebellar dysfunction. Progressive narrowing of base of support and dual-task challenges stress the coordination system adaptively. Vestibular habituation targets BPV/vestibular hypofunction, not cerebellar pathology. Strengthening is adjunctive but not primary.

question_text: A 75-year-old female with a history of 3 falls in 6 months scores 22 seconds on the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test. Which interpretation is CORRECT?
option_a: Score within normal limits for her age group — no intervention required
option_b: Score indicates moderate-to-high fall risk; community-dwelling adults with TUG >12-14 seconds are at increased fall risk
option_c: TUG is not validated in community-dwelling elderly — this result cannot be interpreted
option_d: Score indicates vestibular dysfunction requiring referral to ENT
rationale: TUG normative data: community-dwelling older adults typically complete TUG in <12-13 seconds. A score of >13.5-14 seconds is associated with increased fall risk. A score of 22 seconds indicates significant mobility impairment and high fall risk, warranting targeted fall prevention intervention. The TUG is extensively validated in community-dwelling elderly.

question_text: A new graduate physiotherapist is providing treatment to a patient with a complex condition (post-surgical cardiac and spinal pathology combined) that is outside their current competence. The MOST appropriate action is:
option_a: Treat the patient to the best of their ability as patient access to care must not be delayed
option_b: Decline to treat beyond their competence, seek clinical supervision, and refer to a physiotherapist with appropriate expertise while ensuring care continuity
option_c: Consult with the referring physician by phone and proceed with treatment
option_d: Treat only the spinal component and leave cardiac care entirely to the medical team
rationale: Physiotherapists must practice within their competence. Treating complex combined pathology beyond current competence creates patient safety risk and violates professional standards. The appropriate response is to acknowledge the limitation, seek supervision/mentorship, refer if needed, and ensure the patient is not abandoned. Partial treatment without disclosure of limitation is also inadequate.

question_text: A 48-year-old female presents with 6 months of cervical pain, bilateral upper extremity paresthesia, and gait unsteadiness. MRI shows C4-5 disc herniation with cord compression and increased T2 signal in the spinal cord. Which action is MOST appropriate?
option_a: Begin cervical traction and mobilization to decompress the spinal cord
option_b: Urgently refer to neurosurgery — cervical myelopathy is a surgical emergency requiring decompression
option_c: Begin a conservative cervical stabilization program with manual therapy
option_d: Prescribe a cervical collar and reassess in 6 weeks
rationale: Cervical myelopathy with cord compression, T2 signal changes (indicating cord edema/injury), bilateral symptoms, and gait compromise requires urgent surgical referral for decompression. Conservative management risks progressive and irreversible cord injury. Cervical traction and manual therapy are absolutely contraindicated with cord compression. Collar alone without surgical referral delays necessary care.

question_text: A physiotherapist is performing a muscle energy technique (MET) for a restricted left sacroiliac joint. The patient is asked to isometrically contract against resistance for 7 seconds, then relax. The therapist then takes up the new range. This technique utilizes which neurophysiological mechanism?
option_a: Reciprocal inhibition via Ia afferents
option_b: Post-isometric relaxation via Golgi tendon organ (GTO) activation — autogenic inhibition
option_c: Joint mechanoreceptor stimulation via type I and II receptors
option_d: Central desensitization via gate control theory
rationale: Post-isometric relaxation (PIR) MET: the isometric contraction activates the Golgi tendon organ (GTO/Ib afferents), which produces autogenic inhibition — reflexive relaxation of the contracting muscle, allowing the therapist to gain new range in the post-contraction relaxation window. Reciprocal inhibition involves contraction of the antagonist to relax the agonist.

question_text: A 66-year-old male with COPD (FEV1 45% predicted, GOLD Stage 3) is referred to pulmonary rehabilitation. He reports dyspnea with activities of daily living (mMRC 3). His 6MWT is 280m. After 8 weeks of twice-weekly pulmonary rehab, his 6MWT is 320m. Is this clinically meaningful?
option_a: No — the 40m improvement does not reach the MCID for COPD (MCID 54m)
option_b: Yes — a 40m improvement exceeds the accepted MCID for the 6MWT in COPD (25-35m)
option_c: Unable to determine without post-program spirometry results
option_d: No — improvement must be ≥100m to be clinically relevant in advanced COPD
rationale: The MCID for 6MWT in COPD is approximately 25-35 meters (some sources cite up to 54m for some populations, but 25-35m is the widely accepted standard). A 40m improvement exceeds this threshold and represents a clinically meaningful improvement in exercise capacity. Spirometry does not change with pulmonary rehab, confirming that functional outcomes are the appropriate measure.

question_text: Which of the following BEST describes Evidence-Based Practice (EBP) in physiotherapy?
option_a: Applying only RCT evidence to clinical decisions, superseding clinical experience and patient values
option_b: Integrating best available research evidence with clinical expertise and patient values and preferences
option_c: Following clinical practice guidelines issued by the regulatory college without deviation
option_d: Selecting interventions based on physiotherapist preference and training background
rationale: Sackett's definition of EBP: the conscientious, explicit, and judicious use of current best evidence in making decisions about the care of individual patients, integrated with clinical expertise and patient values. All three elements are required. RCTs alone without clinical context or patient values is not EBP. CPG adherence is component of EBP but not the complete definition.

question_text: A 33-year-old pregnant woman (28 weeks) presents with symphysis pubis pain (5/10) worsening with walking, stair climbing, and single-leg weight-bearing. The MOST appropriate initial management is:
option_a: Aggressive manual therapy to the pubic symphysis and sacroiliac joints
option_b: Activity modification, pelvic girdle belt application, pelvic floor and deep stabilizer exercises, and crutches if needed
option_c: Bed rest for the remainder of the pregnancy
option_d: High-intensity aerobic exercise to maintain fitness and reduce pelvic inflammation
rationale: Pelvic girdle pain (PGP) in pregnancy is managed with activity modification (avoid provocative asymmetric loading), pelvic support belt (trochanteric belt to stabilize the joint), specific exercises targeting deep lumbopelvic stabilizers (transversus abdominis, pelvic floor, gluteus medius), and crutches if weight-bearing is severely affected. Complete bed rest worsens deconditioning and depression.

question_text: A 45-year-old male with ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) presents with progressive upper and lower motor neuron signs, dysarthria, and dysphagia. He currently ambulates independently but has bilateral ankle dorsiflexion weakness. What is the PRIORITY physiotherapy goal?
option_a: Restore lost motor function through intensive progressive resistance training
option_b: Maintain function, prevent complications (contracture, falls, aspiration), and support quality of life through appropriate exercise and assistive devices
option_c: Begin wheelchair prescription immediately as ambulation will decline
option_d: Refer exclusively to palliative care as physiotherapy has no role in ALS management
rationale: ALS is a progressive neurodegenerative disease with no curative treatment. PT goals are to maintain current function as long as possible, prevent secondary complications (joint contracture, falls, pressure injuries), provide appropriate assistive devices proactively, and support QoL. Intensive resisted training aimed at restoration is inappropriate. Early wheelchair prescription before needed is premature. PT has a significant evidence-based role in ALS.

question_text: A patient recovering from COVID-19 (3 months post-acute infection) reports persistent dyspnea on exertion (mMRC 2), fatigue, and cognitive fog. SpO2 at rest is 98% but drops to 91% with a 1-minute sit-to-stand test. Which physiotherapy approach is MOST appropriate?
option_a: High-intensity interval training (HIIT) to rapidly restore cardiovascular fitness
option_b: Pacing and energy conservation strategies, symptom-titrated activity progression, and monitoring for post-exertional malaise
option_c: Complete rest until SpO2 normalizes with all activities
option_d: Breathing retraining with Buteyko technique as primary intervention
rationale: Long COVID management follows a pacing and symptom-titrated approach. Post-exertional malaise (PEM) is a hallmark feature — symptom worsening 12-72 hours after activity — and aggressive exercise can worsen PEM. The physiotherapy approach prioritizes pacing, energy conservation, gradual activity progression below symptom threshold, and monitoring SpO2 during activity. HIIT risks PEM exacerbation.
